content: Tigecycline exhibits a large volume of distribution, ranging from 500 to 700 liters (7 to 9 L/kg), indicating that it is extensively distributed beyond the plasma volume and penetrates into tissues. In a study involving 33 healthy volunteers, tigecycline was administered as a 100 mg initial dose followed by 50 mg every 12 hours. The area under the concentration-time curve (AUC0–12h) in alveolar cells was approximately 134 mcg∙h/mL, which was 78 times higher than the AUC0–12h in serum. The AUC0–12h in epithelial lining fluid was 28 mcg∙h/mL, approximately 32% higher than the serum AUC0–12h. Conversely, the AUC0–12h in skin blister fluid was 61 mcg∙h/mL, approximately 26% lower than the serum AUC0–12h in 10 healthy subjects. In a single-dose study, 100 mg of tigecycline was administered to subjects prior to undergoing elective surgery or medical procedures for tissue extraction. Four hours after administration, tigecycline concentrations were significantly higher in the gallbladder (38-fold), lung (3.7-fold), and colon (2.3-fold) compared to serum levels. However, concentrations were lower in synovial fluid (0.58-fold) and bone (0.35-fold). The distribution of tigecycline in these tissues after multiple doses has not been studied. Tigecycline undergoes minimal metabolism. In vitro studies using human liver microsomes, liver slices, and hepatocytes revealed only trace amounts of metabolites. In healthy male volunteers receiving radiolabeled 14C-tigecycline, the parent compound was the primary labeled material recovered in urine and feces. Minor metabolites, including a glucuronide, an N-acetyl metabolite, and a tigecycline epimer, were each present at no more than 10% of the administered dose. The elimination of tigecycline occurs primarily through biliary and fecal excretion, accounting for 59% of the dose, while 33% is excreted in urine. Approximately 22% of the total dose is excreted as unchanged tigecycline in urine. The primary route of elimination is biliary excretion of unchanged tigecycline and its metabolites, with glucuronidation and renal excretion serving as secondary pathways. Nonclinical toxicology studies have not been conducted to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of tigecycline. However, no mutagenic or clastogenic effects were observed in a series of tests, including in vitro chromosome aberration assays in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells, in vitro forward mutation assays in CHO cells (HGPRT locus), in vitro forward mutation assays in mouse lymphoma cells, and in vivo mouse micronucleus assays. These effects were observed at AUC values of approximately 50 mcg∙hr/mL and 60 mcg∙hr/mL at doses of 30 mg/kg/day and 12 mg/kg/day, respectively. These alterations were shown to be reversible after two weeks of dosing. Tigecycline has been evaluated in adults for the treatment of complicated skin and skin structure infections (cSSSI) in two randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, multinational, multicenter studies (Studies 300 and 305). These studies compared tigecycline (100 mg intravenous initial dose followed by 50 mg every 12 hours) with vancomycin (1 g intravenous every 12 hours) and aztreonam (2 g intravenous every 12 hours) for 5 to 14 days. Patients with complicated deep soft tissue infections, including wound infections, cellulitis (≥10 cm, requiring surgery/drainage or with complicated underlying disease), major abscesses, infected ulcers, and burns, were enrolled. The primary efficacy endpoint was the clinical response at the test of cure (TOC) visit in the clinically evaluable (CE) and clinical modified intent-to-treat (c-mITT) populations. Tigecycline was also evaluated in adults for the treatment of complicated intra-abdominal infections (cIAI) in two randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, multinational, multicenter studies (Studies 301 and 306). These studies compared tigecycline (100 mg intravenous initial dose followed by 50 mg every 12 hours) with imipenem/cilastatin (500 mg intravenous every 6 hours) for 5 to 14 days. Patients with complicated diagnoses, including appendicitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis, gastric/duodenal perforation, intra-abdominal abscess, intestinal perforation, and peritonitis, were enrolled. The primary efficacy endpoint was the clinical response at the TOC visit for the microbiologically evaluable (ME) and microbiologic modified intent-to-treat (m-mITT) populations. For community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP), tigecycline was evaluated in two randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, multinational, multicenter studies (Studies 308 and 313). These studies compared tigecycline (100 mg intravenous initial dose followed by 50 mg every 12 hours) with levofloxacin (500 mg intravenous every 12 or 24 hours). In one study (Study 308), after at least three days of intravenous therapy, a switch to oral levofloxacin (500 mg daily) was permitted for both treatment arms. Total therapy duration ranged from 7 to 14 days. Patients with CABP requiring hospitalization and intravenous therapy were enrolled. The primary efficacy endpoint was the clinical response at the TOC visit in the clinically evaluable (CE) and clinical modified intent-to-treat (c-mITT) populations. Tigecycline is supplied as a lyophilized powder for injection in single-dose 5 mL or 10 mL glass vials, each containing 50 mg of tigecycline. It should be stored at 20°C to 25°C (68°F to 77°F). Patients should be counseled that tigecycline, like other antibacterial drugs, is only effective against bacterial infections and does not treat viral infections (e.g., the common cold). Patients should be advised to complete the full course of therapy as prescribed, even if they feel better early in the treatment course. Skipping doses or not completing the therapy may reduce the effectiveness of the immediate treatment and increase the likelihood of bacterial resistance.
